title: Türkiye Pushes Ceyhan as Alternative Oil Hub as Hormuz Diplomacy Pauses; Saudi Oil Sites Hit by Iraqi Militia Drones
subhead: Ankara is positioning the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan to absorb Gulf crude rerouted around the closed Strait of Hormuz, while a US-Iran diplomatic pause keeps oil prices below $90 and Iranian-backed militias keep striking Saudi oil infrastructure.

sections.heading: Ceyhan Emerges as the Land Bridge Around Hormuz
sections.body:
Türkiye is actively positioning the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan as an alternative outlet for crude that can no longer move through the Strait of Hormuz, according to Anadolu Agency. Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar has said Ankara wants to turn Ceyhan into a 'Rotterdam' — a hub for oil and petroleum products storage, trading and pricing.

The Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline currently moves about 600,000 barrels per day to the terminal, with roughly 400,000 bpd of spare capacity that could push flows toward 1 million bpd. The Iraq-Türkiye Crude Oil Pipeline from Kirkuk has 1.5 million bpd of capacity; Iraq resumed Kirkuk exports through Ceyhan in March and Ankara and Baghdad signed a one-year agreement on Aug. 1 envisaging flows of up to 750,000 bpd. A planned Basra-Haditha line could add up to 2.5 million bpd, giving Ceyhan a theoretical ceiling of 3-3.5 million bpd, roughly 3-3.5% of global demand.
sections.whyItMatters: Ceyhan is becoming the most concrete physical alternative to Hormuz for Gulf and Caspian crude, giving Türkiye and Iraq a strategic hedge against a prolonged closure and reshaping Mediterranean oil trade flows.

sections.heading: Hormuz Diplomacy Pauses as Oil Slides Below $90
sections.body:
The US-Iran conflict remains in a diplomatic pause, with oil prices plunging about 7% on hopes of a reopening, per today's headlines. Al Jazeera reports Tehran has agreed route coordinates with Oman for new shipping lanes through the strait, with Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi saying an understanding covers almost all issues — though large parts of the route would run through Iranian territorial waters. Iran continues to deny direct talks with Washington, insisting negotiations run through Omani mediation.

At Friday's close, Brent stood at $87.07 and WTI at $81.25 per barrel, according to Anadolu citing Baker Hughes data. Traffic through the waterway remains a fraction of normal: Al Jazeera reported as few as eight vessels transiting on some days versus roughly 130 before the war began in late February. US Central Command insists the strait is 'free and open' and says US forces have assisted more than 1,000 vessels in transiting over the past three months.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is pricing a near-term reopening, but the gap between US and Iranian positions on who controls the strait and whether Iran can levy transit fees remains unresolved — leaving prices vulnerable to a sharp reversal if talks collapse.

sections.heading: Saudi Oil Facilities Under Drone Fire From Iraq
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia has been intercepting drones launched from Iraq targeting its oil facilities, with Riyadh blaming Iran-backed Iraqi militias, according to today's headlines. The attacks have extended to Houthi strikes on Saudi oil installations and have rattled Jordan as well, with mediators reporting progress in US-Iran diplomacy even as the regional attacks spread.

This is a widening of the conflict's energy front: rather than a single chokepoint closure, Gulf producers now face a distributed campaign of drone and missile strikes on refining and export infrastructure across multiple countries.
sections.whyItMatters: The attacks test whether Saudi Arabia can keep its own export infrastructure secure even as the main US-Iran confrontation pauses, and they keep a risk premium under Gulf oil regardless of Hormuz diplomacy.

sections.heading: China Acts as the Market's 'Volatility Arbiter'
sections.body:
Goldman Sachs analysts Daan Struyven and Lia Thomas cast Beijing as global commodity markets' de facto 'volatility arbiter', per SCMP. The bank argues Chinese policy dampens price swings in hydrocarbons and gold through price-sensitive import demand, but amplifies volatility in critical metals where China can use supply-chain dominance as leverage in its AI and geopolitical competition with the US.

Goldman says low Chinese crude imports are one reason oil prices have not risen further despite the sharpest supply shock on record, with Beijing acting as a 'swing consumer' — cutting net seaborne crude and LNG imports since March while boosting net exports of organic chemicals and plastics. The bank also estimates China's roughly 20-tonne increase in monthly central bank gold purchases since Russia's reserves were frozen in 2022 has lifted bullion prices by more than 20%.
sections.whyItMatters: China's demand response is quietly doing more to cap oil prices than any OPEC or US policy, while its critical-minerals leverage remains a separate, sharper weapon in the technology supply chain.

sections.heading: US Shale Holds Steady as Rig Count Creeps Up
sections.body:
The US oil rig count rose by 1 to 455 for the week ending Aug. 14, up 43 rigs year-on-year, according to Baker Hughes data reported by Anadolu. The modest increase suggests US producers are adding capacity cautiously even with prices above $80, rather than aggressively chasing the supply gap left by Hormuz disruptions.

The steady rig count, alongside the earlier pivot of Asian refiners toward US crude reported in recent days, points to US barrels absorbing part of the Gulf shortfall — but at a pace that reflects capital discipline and the risk that a Hormuz deal could quickly deflate prices.
sections.whyItMatters: US shale is providing a supply backstop but not a surge, meaning the market remains dependent on either a Hormuz reopening or continued demand destruction to balance.

sections.heading: EU Coal Share Hits Record Low
sections.body:
Coal's share of EU electricity production fell to a record low of 9.2% in 2025, down from more than a third in 1990, according to Eurostat data reported by Anadolu. Hard coal accounted for 3.7% of gross electricity production and brown coal 5.5%, with hard and brown coal consumption hitting new historical lows of 107 million and 184 million tonnes respectively.

The decline comes even as the EU faces energy-security pressures from the Hormuz crisis and the Russia-Ukraine war, underscoring that the bloc's structural shift away from coal has continued through the supply shocks rather than reversing.
sections.whyItMatters: The EU's coal phase-down is now structural and largely irreversible, which tightens the bloc's reliance on gas, nuclear and renewables at a moment of heightened import-security risk.

bottomLine: The most concrete energy development today is not in the Gulf but on Türkiye's Mediterranean coast: Ceyhan is being built up as a land bridge for crude rerouted around a closed Hormuz, with Iraq already shifting Kirkuk flows through it. Meanwhile the US-Iran diplomatic pause has oil trading below $90 on hopes of a reopening, even as Iranian-backed militias keep striking Saudi oil infrastructure and China's demand response quietly caps prices. The market is betting on a deal; the physical infrastructure is being built as if it may not come.
sources: Anadolu Agency, Al Jazeera, SCMP, Goldman Sachs, Baker Hughes, Eurostat, Reuters headlines
